n: Joseph and Oliver disagreed about whether the Apostle John had died. Through the Urim and Thummim they received this translated version of a record John himself wrote, in which John recounts Jesus asking what he most desired.

f.g: John the Apostle, often called “the disciple whom Jesus loved.”

f.w: if you shall ask what you will, it shall be granted unto you

n: John asks for power over death so he can keep living and bringing souls to Christ — the same wish later granted to three Nephite disciples.
Because of this desire, John will “tarry” — remain on earth — until Christ comes in glory, prophesying to every nation and people.

f.w: prophesy before nations, kindreds, tongues and people

n: This explains Jesus’ cryptic words to Peter in John 21: “If I will that he tarry till I come, what is that to thee?” John wanted to bring souls to Christ; Peter wanted to come quickly to Christ’s kingdom.

f.w: If I will that he tarry till I come, what is that to thee?

n: Jesus assures Peter that his desire was good, but John chose to do an even greater work among people.
John will be like flaming fire and a ministering angel, serving those on earth who will inherit salvation.

f.w: as flaming fire and a ministering angel

n: Peter will minister alongside John and his brother James, holding the keys of this ministry until Christ comes. Peter, James, and John later restored the Melchizedek Priesthood to Joseph and Oliver.

f.w: unto you three I will give this power and the keys of this ministry

n: Both Peter and John receive what they desired, and both rejoice in their choices. God honors different righteous desires.

f.w: ye shall both have according to your desires
